description: The 19 logo designers who defined the craft, the designers and studios working today, and how to judge, brief and hire one for your own brand.
body:
Searching for the best logo designer usually means one of two things.

Either you want to know who shaped this craft, or you need to hire someone this quarter and you are trying to work out what good looks like.

This guide answers both, in that order.

I am Arek Dvornechuck, a senior freelance brand identity and web designer in Brooklyn, and I have spent over 20 years designing marks, including a period working with Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv.

I compiled this list, I verified every living designer and studio on it in October 2026, and I removed the ones whose practices no longer exist.

How to use this list

The first section is the canon: nineteen designers whose marks you already know, with the specific decision that made each one work.

Read it as a vocabulary rather than as trivia, because those decisions are what you will be judging in a real portfolio.

The second section covers designers and studios working today, every one checked against their live site this month.

The rest is the part most roundups leave out: how to judge a portfolio, what a real process looks like, what you should receive at handoff, what to ask, and what it costs.

This article is deliberately global, so if you are specifically looking for someone local, I keep a separate guide to the best logo and brand identity designers in NYC.

19 of the best logo designers of all time

These are not ranked, because a ranking between Paul Rand and Milton Glaser would be a marketing device rather than a judgement.

  1. Paul Rand — IBM
  2. Ivan Chermayeff — Showtime
  3. Tom Geismar — Mobil
  4. Sagi Haviv — Library of Congress
  5. Paula Scher — Citi
  6. Steff Geissbuhler — Time Warner Cable
  7. Milton Glaser — I Love NY
  8. Rob Janoff — Apple
  9. Lindon Leader — FedEx
  10. Tinker Hatfield — Air Jordan
  11. Otto Firle — Lufthansa
  12. James Modarelli — NASA
  13. Henri Kay Henrion — KLM
  14. Frank Mason Robinson — Coca-Cola
  15. Alan Fletcher — V&A
  16. Anton Stankowski — Deutsche Bank
  17. Carolyn Davidson — Nike
  18. Raymond Loewy — Shell
  19. Salvador Dalí — Chupa Chups

1. Paul Rand — IBM

Paul Rand was the American art director who turned corporate identity into a discipline.

His IBM logo, with its eight horizontal stripes, suggests speed and dynamism while working as a mnemonic device.

His work for IBM, UPS, ABC and NeXT set the standard every identity designer still measures against.

Rand argued that a logo should be simple, memorable and timeless, and that a client is buying judgement rather than drawings.

2. Ivan Chermayeff — Showtime

Ivan Chermayeff co-founded the New York firm now known as Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv.

His Showtime logo pulls the network’s abbreviation out of its own name, so the shorthand people already used became the mark.

His work is a long argument that a bold, simple form can carry a complicated idea without explaining itself.

3. Tom Geismar — Mobil

Tom Geismar founded that same firm with Chermayeff, and at 95 he is still its founding partner.

His designs for Mobil, Xerox, Chase Manhattan Bank and PBS are among the most reproduced marks in the world.

The Mobil logo puts a single red o inside an otherwise neutral wordmark, which fixes the pronunciation and the memory at once.

Geismar’s work is the clearest proof that a small, deliberate decision can carry an entire identity.

4. Sagi Haviv — Library of Congress

Sagi Haviv joined Chermayeff & Geismar in 2003 and is now a partner and designer there.

His Library of Congress mark turns an open book into a waving flag, two ideas held in one shape.

He is also the most useful living designer to study if you want to hear how an identity is argued for, not just presented.

5. Paula Scher — Citi

Paula Scher has been a partner in Pentagram’s New York office since 1991.

Her Citi logo, famously sketched during the first client meeting, folds the old Travelers umbrella into a single red arc over the t.

Her identity work for The Public Theater and Tiffany & Co. shows typography treated as the loudest element in a brand, not the quiet one.

You can see the thinking behind marks like this in my collection of original logo sketches.

6. Steff Geissbuhler — Time Warner Cable

Steff Geissbuhler was a partner and principal at Chermayeff & Geismar for three decades.

His Time Warner Cable mark combines an eye and an ear into one pictograph, which is about as literal as communication design gets without becoming a diagram.

His work is a reminder that a symbol can state what a company does and still be worth looking at.

7. Milton Glaser — I Love NY

Milton Glaser was the American designer behind the I ♥ NY mark and the psychedelic Bob Dylan poster.

He was the first graphic designer to receive the National Medal of Arts.

The I ♥ NY logo was drawn for a tourism campaign and became the most imitated piece of graphic design ever made, which is its own kind of lesson about ownership.

He died in 2020, on his ninety-first birthday.

8. Rob Janoff — Apple

Rob Janoff drew the Apple logo in 1977 as a young art director.

The bite was there to stop the shape reading as a cherry at small sizes, which is a craft decision rather than a concept.

It is the best-known example of the rule that a mark has to survive the size you will actually use it at.

9. Lindon Leader — FedEx

Lindon Leader created the FedEx mark in 1994 while senior design director at Landor Associates.

The arrow formed by the negative space between the E and the x reads as forward motion, speed and precision.

Leader reportedly worked through hundreds of letterform variations to get that gap to behave, which is the part of the story most people skip.

The idea was free; the execution took months.

10. Tinker Hatfield — Air Jordan

Tinker Hatfield shaped the Air Jordan line at Nike from the Air Jordan III onward.

The Jumpman silhouette, traced from a photograph of Michael Jordan, became the emblem that carried the line.

It is the clearest demonstration that a silhouette can hold a brand when the thing it depicts is already famous.

11. Otto Firle — Lufthansa

Otto Firle was a German architect and designer who drew the crane emblem for Deutsche Luft-Reederei in 1918.

That airline later became Lufthansa, a name that joins Luft (air) with Hansa, a reference to the Hanseatic League.

The crane has survived more than a century with only small refinements, which is the rarest outcome in this entire field.

12. James Modarelli — NASA

James Modarelli designed the NASA insignia in 1959, the year after the agency was founded.

Known as the meatball, it holds a sphere for a planet, stars for space, a red chevron for aeronautics and an orbiting spacecraft.

It breaks almost every rule of modern simplicity and still works, because the audience was never asked to decode it.

13. Henri Kay Henrion — KLM

Henri Kay Henrion was a German-born British designer and one of the founders of modern European corporate identity.

His KLM identity places a crown above the airline’s initials, borrowing authority from the Dutch royal title without illustrating it.

He wrote about identity as a management problem long before most clients were ready to hear it.

14. Frank Mason Robinson — Coca-Cola

Frank Mason Robinson was a bookkeeper rather than a designer.

He suggested the name Coca-Cola in 1886 and wrote it in the Spencerian script that was standard business handwriting at the time.

That accident of penmanship is now one of the most valuable pieces of lettering in the world, which should make every designer humble about where good marks come from.

15. Alan Fletcher — V&A

Alan Fletcher was called "the most highly regarded graphic designer of his generation" by The Daily Telegraph.

His Victoria and Albert Museum mark removes a leg of the A and tucks it into the ampersand, without losing a letter of legibility.

He was a founding partner of Pentagram, and his work is the best argument that wit is a professional tool, not a distraction.

16. Anton Stankowski — Deutsche Bank

Anton Stankowski was a German designer who pioneered constructive graphic art.

His Deutsche Bank mark is a slash inside a square: the slash reads as growth, the square as containment and safety.

It is the cleanest example in this list of an abstract mark that still has a stated meaning.

17. Carolyn Davidson — Nike

Carolyn Davidson drew the Nike swoosh in 1971 while still a student at Portland State.

The fluid shape suggests motion and speed, which is roughly all a running-shoe company needs its mark to do.

Phil Knight’s famous first reaction was that he did not love it but he would grow to like it.

Great marks are rarely loved on the day they are presented, which is worth remembering when you review your own.

18. Raymond Loewy — Shell

Raymond Loewy was a French-born American industrial designer whose work ran from locomotives to logos.

He refined the Shell pecten into the flatter, bolder version introduced in 1971, which is still essentially the mark in use today.

His own principle, that a design should be the most advanced thing an audience is still ready to accept, is the most useful sentence in this entire article.

19. Salvador Dalí — Chupa Chups

Salvador Dalí, the Spanish surrealist, designed the Chupa Chups logo in 1969.

He set the name inside a bright daisy shape and told the company to put it on top of the lollipop rather than the side, so it is always the right way up.

The placement decision mattered more than the drawing, which is true far more often than designers like to admit.

Two things connect all nineteen.

None of these marks explains the business.

And every one of them was drawn to survive a specific physical constraint — a truck, a tail fin, a lollipop, a letterhead, a favicon before favicons existed.

If you want the wider history of the field rather than logos specifically, I have a companion list of famous graphic designers.

Logo designers and studios working today

Everyone below has a live site and current work, checked in October 2026.

I have excluded several names that still circulate on other roundups, because their sites are now parked, empty or reduced to a splash page.

Naming someone you cannot actually hire is the most common failure in lists like this one.

Independent designers you can study or commission

Sagi Haviv and Tom Geismar still run Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv from West 24th Street in Manhattan, with principal designers Mackey Saturday and Melanie McElduff.

Recent work includes the U.S. Open, NBC, America250 and the 2026 rebrand of Mercy Corps as Prosper Global.

This is the closest thing to a direct line from the canon above to a firm you can commission today.

Paula Scher is still a serving partner at Pentagram in New York, running her own team inside the firm.

Her identity and environmental work is the reference point for anyone who wants type to do the heavy lifting.

Michael Bierut joined Pentagram’s New York office as a partner in 1990 and moved to an advisory role there in October 2024.

His clients have included Mastercard, Slack, Verizon, Benetton and Disney, and he created the typographic inscription on the Obama Presidential Center.

If you only read one designer on how clients actually behave, read him.

Aaron Draplin runs Draplin Design Co., which is one person, a deep archive and a famously unfashionable work ethic.

His site publishes a logo archive, a logo process and a logo graveyard — the rejected work as well as the approved work.

That graveyard is the single most useful free resource on this page for understanding what a logo project really costs in effort.

Jessica Hische is a lettering artist and designer in Oakland whose practice covers lettering, logos and branding, books and typefaces.

Her client work includes Starbucks, Neiman Marcus and Simon & Schuster.

She is the person to study if your brand needs a custom wordmark rather than a symbol.

Radim Malinic runs Brand Nu, an independent branding studio in Mayfair, London, working with clients worldwide.

Recent projects include Lux Coffee Co., Vixen & Fox and Harnham.

He also writes openly about the business of running a design practice, which is rarer than it should be.

Identity studios with international reach

These are the firms a large company short-lists when the brief is a repositioning rather than a logo.

Pentagram calls itself the world’s largest independent design consultancy, with 23 partners across New York, London, Austin and Berlin.

Recent work includes the Obama Presidential Center, Isomorphic Labs and the Guggenheim.

Every partner runs an independent team, so you are choosing a partner, not a company.

Koto works from Los Angeles, New York, London, Berlin and Sydney, and has rebranded Instagram, Amazon and Tripadvisor.

Its Amazon engagement ran 18 months across 15 markets and more than 50 sub-brands, which is a useful scale marker when you are told a rebrand is quick.

Wolff Olins is a global brand consultancy with offices in London, New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Recent clients include Blank Street, Lloyds and Decathlon.

Its work is usually bought for repositioning rather than for a logo.

Collins organizes its offer around commercial outcomes — repositioning, premiumization, turnaround, exit — rather than around deliverables.

Its clients include Red Wing Shoes, Bose and the San Francisco Symphony.

Read the way it frames a brief even if you never hire it, because that framing is what senior work sounds like.

Studio Dumbar works from Rotterdam and has collaborated with OpenAI’s brand and product design teams since 2024.

Its other work includes Apple Football, Meta Connect and Feyenoord.

It is now part of DEPT®, so it is a studio inside a larger group rather than a fully independent practice.

Base Design runs studios in New York, Brussels, Geneva, Melbourne and Saigon.

Its projects include MOCA Los Angeles, Birkenstock, DashPass by DoorDash and the Grand Palais.

Turner Duckworth works from London, New York and San Francisco, and is best known for the Coca-Cola and Amazon identity work.

It also designed the Metallica identity, which is a useful example of a logo system for something other than a company.

It recruits through Publicis Groupe, so treat it as a network studio rather than an independent one.

Further is the agency formerly called DesignStudio, with offices in London, Brooklyn and Dubai.

Its clients include UFC, Eurostar, Airbnb, Xbox and EA Sports.

If you find an old list recommending DesignStudio, this is where that firm went.

How to judge a logo designer’s portfolio

Most people look at a portfolio and ask whether they like it, which is the least useful question available.

Here is what I look at instead, in order.

Look for complete projects, not single images.

A designer who can only show a logo on a dark square has either not finished the work or did not do all of it.

Check whether the mark survives one colour and small sizes.

Ask to see the favicon, the embroidered version, the single-colour print version — the places where a weak mark falls apart.

Read the credits honestly.

Working on a project at an agency is not the same as having designed it, and a good designer will tell you exactly which part was theirs if you ask.

Look for range in the thinking, not in the style.

Three projects that look identical usually means one aesthetic applied to three different businesses, which is a problem you will inherit.

Find the project closest to your actual problem.

An exact industry match matters far less than a matching challenge: a launch, a repositioning, a complicated product, a brand that has to work in a physical space.

If you want the criteria from the other side of the table, I wrote about what makes a strong logo design portfolio.

What a good logo design process looks like

A real process has a shape you can see before the work starts, and it always begins with questions rather than sketches.

1. Discovery.

The designer should ask about your customers, your competitors, your positioning and what you want people to think — before showing you anything visual.

2. Exploration.

Sketching happens on paper or in rough form, and the volume here is what makes the final mark feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

3. A small number of real directions.

Two or three considered routes beat twelve variations, because twelve options is a sign the designer is asking you to do the deciding.

4. Refinement against the real world.

The chosen direction gets drawn properly, tested at every size, and put on the things you actually use.

5. The system.

Colour, typography, layout rules and a guideline document turn a logo into something a team can use without calling the designer.

My own version of this runs as a one-week sprint, and I have written it up step by step in my logo design process guide.

What you should receive at handoff

This is the single most useful thing to agree in writing before you pay a deposit.

A complete handoff should include all of the following.

  • Vector master artwork in SVG, EPS or AI, which is the only version that can be scaled or re-coloured later.
  • Exported files in PNG and PDF, for screen and print, including transparent versions.
  • Every approved lockup: primary, horizontal, stacked, symbol alone, and a single-colour version.
  • Colour values in HEX, RGB, CMYK and Pantone, so print and screen do not drift apart.
  • Typography: the actual typefaces, with the licence you are expected to buy named explicitly.
  • Brand guidelines covering clear space, minimum size and what people are not allowed to do to the mark.
  • Full ownership of the final artwork, assigned to you in writing.

Ownership is the one people forget.

If the contract does not transfer the rights to the final mark, you have bought a licence to use your own logo.

For what a complete identity package contains beyond the mark itself, see my branding package breakdown and these brand guidelines examples.

Questions to ask before you hire

Ask these on the first call, and listen for whether the answers are specific.

Who will actually design this?

At an agency the person pitching is often not the person drawing, and that is worth knowing before you sign.

What exactly is included, and what is extra?

Get the deliverable list in writing, including the number of directions and the number of revision rounds.

What happens if I do not like any of the first directions?

A confident designer has a clear answer to this; an evasive one is telling you how the project will end.

How long will it take, and what do you need from me?

Most overruns are caused by slow client feedback, so the designer should tell you your own deadlines too.

Do I own the final artwork outright?

The answer should be yes, in writing, with no conditions attached to future use.

Can I speak to a recent client?

A designer with a real practice will offer a reference without hesitating.

Freelancer, studio, agency or marketplace?

These four options are not four price points for the same thing — they are genuinely different products.

A marketplace or contest site gives you a mark quickly and cheaply, drawn by someone who will never speak to you.

There is no strategy, the research is skipped, originality is not checked, and you will often receive files you cannot use at scale.

It is a reasonable choice when the business itself is still an experiment.

A senior freelancer gives you the person who does the work, with no account layer and no internal handoffs.

You get speed and direct access, and the limit is capacity: one person can only run so many projects at once.

A small studio adds a second or third specialist, usually a strategist or a developer, at a higher cost and a slower pace.

This is the right shape when the identity has to launch alongside packaging, a site and a campaign at the same moment.

A large agency gives you research depth, process and the ability to coordinate a rollout across many markets.

You also pay for an account team, and the senior name you met in the pitch may not be the person drawing your logo.

The honest summary: if you are a founder or a small team, the most common mistake is overbuying the agency and underbuying the thinking.

Red flags worth walking away from

Any one of these is a reason to pause, and two together is a reason to leave.

  • Unlimited revisions. It sounds generous and it means there is no decision-making process at all.
  • No questions before the first designs. If nobody asked about your customers, the mark is decoration.
  • A portfolio of mockups only. Rendered scenes with no real client, no credit and no outcome usually mean unpaid concepts.
  • Work you can find on a stock icon site. Reverse image search the three marks you like most; it takes a minute.
  • No contract, or no written scope. Every dispute I have ever heard about started here.
  • Vector files withheld until a later payment. Staged payment is fine; withholding the master artwork as leverage is not.
  • A price with no scope attached. A number without a deliverable list is not a quote.
  • Pressure to decide today. Good designers are busy, not desperate.

What a good logo designer costs

Price tracks scope and seniority, and almost nothing else.

A marketplace mark can be under a hundred dollars, an experienced freelancer is usually in the low thousands, a studio in the tens of thousands, and a global agency rebrand runs into six or seven figures.

Those numbers are not measuring the same deliverable, which is why comparing them directly is useless.

I have broken the whole range down, with what you actually get at each level, in my logo design cost guide.

The famous numbers people quote are worse than useless, because almost every one of them describes a different kind of engagement.

My own answer is a flat $3,000 per week, with a complete brand identity delivered in one week and larger projects quoted as a fixed number of weeks agreed before anything starts.

There is no hourly billing and revisions are included — the full breakdown is on my pricing page.

Compare proposals on scope, seniority and ownership, never on the headline number.

Work with me on your identity

I am a freelance designer, which means the person you meet on the call is the person who draws the mark.

For Airport Executive, a London chauffeur service under new ownership, I built an aviation-inspired monogram and carried it through print, a chauffeur badge, signage and a new website.

For Fox Berman, a law firm in Sint Maarten, I drew a custom wordmark with precise inktraps and paired it with a vivid orange that the Caribbean context earned.

For SweetGrass, a cannabis dispensary in Mississippi, the identity started from Art Deco lettering and ran through bespoke type, patterns and packaging.

For Aero, a breath-analysis company, the brief was the opposite: a clinical lowercase wordmark and a lab-grade palette that make precision feel approachable.

Those are four different problems and four different answers, which is the only portfolio argument I think is worth making.

You can see the full range of services, and if the fit looks right, book a call and tell me what you are building.

Logo designer FAQ

Who is the best logo designer of all time?

There is no single answer, but Paul Rand is the name most designers give.

He designed IBM, UPS, ABC and NeXT, and he established the idea that a corporate mark is a business asset rather than decoration.

Milton Glaser, Tom Geismar and Alan Fletcher have equally strong claims, and any ranking between them says more about taste than merit.

How do I find a good logo designer?

Start from complete projects rather than single images.

Shortlist three designers whose work solves a problem close to yours, read the project credits to confirm who actually did the work, and then talk to each one about your brief.

Compare their written proposals on scope, seniority, deliverables and ownership before you compare the prices.

What should a logo designer deliver at the end of a project?

Vector master artwork, exports for screen and print, and every approved lockup.

That means SVG or EPS files, PNG and PDF exports, primary and stacked and single-colour versions, colour values in HEX, RGB, CMYK and Pantone, named typefaces with licensing, brand guidelines, and written transfer of ownership to you.

How much does it cost to hire a professional logo designer?

An experienced freelancer typically charges in the low thousands for a logo and identity system.

Marketplace sites sit under a few hundred dollars, small studios in the tens of thousands, and global agency rebrands reach six or seven figures.

I charge a flat $3,000 per week, with a full brand identity delivered in one week.

Should I hire a freelancer or an agency?

Hire a freelancer when you want the senior person doing the work and you want to move quickly.

Hire an agency when the rollout spans many markets or teams and you need project management as much as design.

The usual mistake for founders and small teams is paying agency rates for work a senior freelancer would do better and faster.

How long does a logo design project take?

Anywhere from one week to three months, depending on scope and on how fast you give feedback.

A focused identity sprint can finish in a week, a studio engagement usually runs six to twelve weeks, and a large agency rebrand runs for months.

Slow client decisions are the most common cause of overruns, not slow designers.

Do I own the logo once I have paid for it?

Only if the contract says so in writing.

Ownership of final artwork should be assigned to you on final payment, with no restrictions on future use.

Fonts are separate: typefaces are licensed, not transferred, so your agreement should name the licence you need to buy and who buys it.

Can AI design a logo for me instead?

AI can generate a mark, but it cannot make the decisions that give a mark value.

It does not research your competitors, cannot tell you when a shape is already owned by someone else, and does not produce the production files or the system around the logo.

It is a useful sketching tool and a poor substitute for judgement.

Final thoughts

The nineteen designers at the top of this page have almost nothing in common stylistically.

What they share is that each one made one decision that could be explained in a sentence and then executed it with more care than the brief required.

That is also the test for the designer you hire: can they tell you, in plain words, why the mark is that shape?

If they can, the price will usually look reasonable, and if they cannot, no budget will fix it.

When you are ready to talk about your own identity, book a call.
